name: Isaac Newton
role: English natural philosopher; MP for Cambridge University (1689-1690, 1701-1702); Warden then Master of the Royal Mint (1696-1727)
summary: Newton was a scientist whose political record is thin. He was tied to the Whigs, sat briefly in Parliament, and as Mint official oversaw the Great Recoinage, prosecuted counterfeiters and wrote the 1717 report that led to Britain's de facto gold standard. His heterodox anti-Trinitarian beliefs were kept private and no stated position on church and state or on government form was found.

death-penalty.rationale: No recorded view on capital punishment; prosecuting counterfeiters as Warden of the Mint is something nearby.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In his Seven Statements on Religion he held that 'the laws of God & the laws of man are to be kept distinct' and that men's commandments are not to be made 'a part of the laws of God'; he does not argue that civil law be drawn from scripture.

separate-church-state.rationale: In his Seven Statements on Religion he wrote 'That Religion & polity or the laws of God & the laws of man are to be kept distinct. We are not [to] make the commandments of men a part of the laws of God', and in Irenicum that imposing as an article of communion what was not one from the first preaching of the Gospel, and 'the persecuting of any true Christians for not receiving' it, is 'persecuting Christ in his mystical members' and makes a church 'Antichristian'.

universal-morality.rationale: In his Short Scheme of the True Religion he wrote that 'there is but one law for all nations the law of righteousness & charity dictated to the Christians by Christ to the Iews by Moses & to all mankind by the light of reason', by which all men are judged.

notes: Later pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-11-14): brought to rules 7 and deepened. The October audit left every statement null after an early exit; this pass reads three of his own religious papers on the Newton Project (Seven Statements on Religion, A Short Scheme of the True Religion, Irenicum) and answers separate-church-state, laws-from-scripture and universal-morality. His Mint work (the Great Recoinage, prosecutions of coiners, the 1717 report on gold) and his two terms as MP are recorded in the sources already cited and bear on no statement here without an inference. The four Gutenberg books (Observations on Daniel, Chronology, Opticks, Principia) are declined in booksNotUsed.
